0.1.n: This is the item being defined, not a name.

0.3.n: Marks 書見台 as the topic of the definition.

0.4.n: Refers to documents or other materials supported by the stand.

0.5.n: Marks 資料 as what becomes easier to read.

0.6.n: 読む combines with やすい; its linking form やすく connects to なる.

0.7.n: Follows 読みやすく to describe a change in readability.

0.8.n: Together with に, introduces the intended result: making materials easier to read.

0.9.n: Completes ように, connecting the intended result to the stand’s design.

1.0.n: Names the surface where the stand is placed.

1.1.n: Links 机 to 上, identifying the desk’s top.

1.2.n: Combines with 机の to specify the surface of the desk.

1.3.n: Marks the location where something is placed with 置く.

1.4.n: The て-form of 置く links placement on the desk to the following description.

1.5.n: Describes an angle that stays constant.

1.6.n: Connects 一定 to 角度, making it describe the angle.

1.7.n: Refers to the tilt at which the materials are held.

1.8.n: Marks the angle maintained by 保持.

1.9.n: A formal noun that combines with できる to express the ability to keep something in place.

1.10.n: With 保持, expresses what the stand allows someone to do.

1.11.n: Part of ようにした, describing how the stand was designed.

1.12.n: Connects よう to した in a pattern expressing an intentionally enabled result.

1.13.n: Past form of する; ようにした describes something made to allow the preceding action.

1.14.n: The preceding description tells us what kind of support this is.

1.16.n: Casual equivalent of と, marking the definition as quoted text.

1.17.n: 書く in the てある form describes text that has been written and remains there.

1.18.n: Short for の; adds an explanatory tone before です.

1.19.n: Makes the explanation polite as part of んです.

1.20.n: Softly leads from the written definition into the speaker’s own reason for buying it.

2.0.n: Softens the rejected explanation; というより supplies the contrast rather than an explicit negative verb.

2.1.n: The speaker explicitly identifies herself as the buyer.

2.2.n: Marks 私 as the topic, shifting from the definition to personal experience.

2.3.n: Refers to books generally, contrasting with the textbooks mentioned next.

2.4.n: Marks 本 as what the speaker would read.

2.5.n: 読む becomes 読みたい; its て-form 読みたくて presents the desire as a possible reason for buying.

2.6.n: Plain past form of 買う, inside the explanation being reconsidered.

2.7.n: Casual と before いう, framing the preceding buying explanation as an idea.

2.8.n: In っていうより, it frames a description rather than reporting literal speech.

2.9.n: Introduces a comparison between this explanation and the more accurate one that follows.

2.10.n: Emphasizes the contrast in よりは; the preferred explanation comes next.

3.0.n: 授業 plus 中 refers to the time while a lesson is taking place.

3.1.n: Marks 授業中 as the time for placing the textbook.

3.2.n: Specifies the reading materials the speaker actually wants to support.

3.3.n: Marks 教科書 as what will be placed on the stand.

3.4.n: The dictionary form comes before ために to state the intended use.

3.5.n: Following 置く, it forms a purpose expression with に.

3.6.n: Completes ために, explaining what the speaker wants the stand for.

3.7.n: An adjective expressing desire for a thing; the desired stand is left unstated.

3.8.n: Adds a soft, wistful tone to the speaker’s internal thought.

3.10.n: Marks 欲しいな as the thought reported by 思っていて.

3.11.n: Shows that the desire persisted before the purchase.

3.12.n: 思う in the ongoing ている form, then linked with て to the eventual purchase.

3.14.n: Polite past form of 買う, stating the final action.

0.lit: As for a bookstand, so that materials become easy to read,
0.tip: Verb stem + やすい means easy to do; 読みやすくなる means become easier to read.

1.lit: A stand placed on a desk, made to hold at a fixed angle—that’s written, but…
1.tip: って書いてある introduces what written text says; って is the casual quotation marker.

2.lit: Not particularly, as for me, rather than saying I bought it wanting to read books,
2.tip: っていうよりは means rather than saying that, introducing a more accurate explanation next.

3.lit: To place textbooks during class, I’d long been thinking, I want it, and bought it.
3.tip: A dictionary-form verb + ために expresses purpose: 置くために means in order to place.
